b: In this episode, Peter welcomes back Nav Chandel, a distinguished professor and world-renowned expert in mitochondrial biology, for a conversation that challenges many conventional assumptions about mitochondria and their role in health and aging. Nav begins by explaining what mitochondria do beyond ATP production, emphasizing their critical role in cellular communication and signaling. He explores how mitochondria communicate through hydrogen peroxide, metabolites, and mitochondrial DNA and RNA, and how these signals influence inflammation, immune function, and epigenetic regulation. The conversation then turns to the relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and aging, including what the term “mitochondrial dysfunction” actually means and why it is often misused. Drawing on his own research, Nav takes a deep dive into metformin, explaining its effects on mitochondrial function, metabolism, and inflammation. He examines the evidence for its potential benefits in preventing age-related diseases and why findings from cancer trials have been disappointing. Finally, Nav offers an evidence-based assessment of popular mitochondrial supplements and interventions, including urolithin A, alpha-ketoglutarate, methylene blue, and hyperbaric oxygen. Throughout the discussion, Peter and Nav separate established science from speculation, providing a clearer understanding of mitochondrial biology and its implications for health and longevity.

Peter had Nav on the podcast 7 years ago [episode #31], and there’s so much new stuff to talk about
He always likes to ground people in what the mitochondria are

Unfortunately, mitochondria has become one of the top 10 buzzwords on social media, so there’s no chance that anybody listening or watching us hasn’t heard the term, but that second and third order understanding might be a little foggy
It’s not only mitochondria, but the other big buzzword is mitochondrial dysfunction
So if you’re going to talk about mitochondrial dysfunction, why don’t we start with mitochondrial function?
We are NOT going to discuss how mitochondria are made or degraded and how many different kinds of mitochondria there may be.
We’re going to focus on one thing: mitochondrial function

Most people know mitochondria as the powerhouse of the cell because it makes the ATP and that gives you the power for your muscles, your neurons to fire, and for a long time, most of us just thought about mitochondria as an ATP generator
“When mitochondrial dysfunction comes, does it happen in aging or in heart failure? It’s you don’t make enough ATP.”‒ Nav Chandel
Now remember, glycolysis can also make ATP, but mitochondria is much more efficient and can give you a lot more
It’s very simple, and all the great theories around mitochondrial dysfunction related to any particular disease (if it is causal) or the natural aging process is all about ATP
Nav is NOT going to talk about the ATP because there’s a lot more that mitochondria do
To back up, the electron transport chain generates a protomotive force, basically a voltage which can be harnessed to make ATP
That process is coupled to something called the Krebs cycle (or the TCA cycle), and it turns out that the TCA cycle is the anabolic engine also in your cells

1 – Mitochondria make 2 things: make ATP and make the building blocks (the metabolites) for new lipids, new nucleotides (like DNA, RNA), new amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) ‒ people forgot that mitochondria is an anabolic engine
We’ll get into it with cancer in a second
That’s what classically, the great biochemist of the 20th century taught us, and that’s what’s in your textbooks
What has changed in the last 30 years
And Nav has been part of that revolution
They’re just not an organelle sitting on the side, and things like mTOR, when they get activated or deactivated (mTOR is a big decision maker of metabolism)
Your genes being turned on and off, they’re deciding cell fate, how a cell becomes what it does
The paradigm that mitochondria is just sitting there giving you ATP, giving you metabolites (it has no decision-making properties) ‒ that has changed
Let’s back up and give folks a sense of size and scale
Are there any cells in the body that don’t have mitochondria?
Absent red blood cells, when you consider all the other cells which have mitochondria, what is the approximate cellular density of mitochondria?
Hepatocytes are full of them ‒ we’re talking thousands, maybe more

Instead of worrying about are they dense or they’re not dense, if you look at them from what they’re doing:
There’s the ATP
There’s the metabolites

But what Nav really wants to get into is the third aspect which a few mitochondria could probably fulfill
And so that way, you don’t have to always think about mitochondrial biogenesis.
Peter is thinking more in terms of supply and demand mismatch
For example, are they being paired to cells in density based on energy need or metabolite need?

Because for example, a hepatocyte doesn’t actually need much ATP, but it needs a lot of anabolic precursor
It makes glucose, for example

Peter assumes that in the hepatocyte, the density is optimized more towards anabolism, whereas in a very energy dense cell like a muscle cell where ATP is probably more important than precursor to building blocks, you’re optimizing around this other function of ATP generation ‒ that’s what Peter was asking about
On a first approximation, that’s true, although because there’s a third function, that simple theory, Nav doesn’t disagree with that
“I just don’t think about it anymore in those simple terms because there’s a third function that is becoming very dominant.”‒ Nav Chandel

And Nav actually doesn’t know how this third function (that he’s going to talk about) fits into that paradigm that Peter just explained, and that’s why he’s stopped thinking about more or less mitochondria
Mitochondria are constantly generating signals to the rest of the cell
These signals are optimized for cellular function

One of them is the electron transport chain is not a perfect system and it leaks electrons
It can leak a little bit of electrons or a lot of electrons to make H2O2 (it makes superoxide first and then H2O2)

People used to think H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide) in cells is damaging, damaging, damaging
The oldest theory of aging says that as you get older, your mitochondria degenerate and they make copious amounts of H2O2 to cause degeneration of the muscle, of the neuron

Navdeep (Nav) Chandel earned a BA in Mathematics and Ph.D. in Cell Physiology from the University of Chicago. In 2000 he started his laboratory at Northwestern University on the concept of mitochondria as signaling organelles. Dr. Chandel is the David W. Cugell Professor of Medicine (Pulmonary and Critical Care), Biochemistry and Molecular genetics at the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University. His research focuses on understanding the function of mitochondria beyond the production of metabolites and ATP. He has characterized the role of mitochondria in cellular signaling through the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and other metabolites. In the field of cancer, his work established mitochondrial metabolism and ROS as necessary for tumorigenesis. Dr. Chandel is part of the Tumor Environment and Metastasis Team in the Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center of Northwestern University.

Dr. Chandel is a world renowned expert in mitochondria and metabolism. He authored a widely utilized introductory book, Navigating Metabolism. He has published over 300 peer reviewed papers. He received the Clarence Ver Steeg Faculty Mentor Award in 2013. In 2023, he was the co-recipient of the Lurie Prize in Biomedical Sciences given by the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH). [Chandel Lab]
